title: Explain common operating system (OS) types and their purposes
tip: Filesystem-to-OS matching is the trap here — students default to 'NTFS everywhere.' Know which filesystem belongs to which OS natively, and why ext4/XFS/APFS aren't interchangeable with NTFS.
checklist: Windows / Linux / macOS / Chrome OS (workstation OSs)

recall.q: A technician needs to format a USB drive that will move large (>10GB) video files between a Windows PC and a Mac. Which filesystem should they choose?
Which filesystem is the native, journaling filesystem for modern macOS?
A vendor announces a product has reached EOL. What's the practical support risk a technician should flag to a customer still running it?
recall.a: No more security patches or vendor support — known vulnerabilities stay unpatched indefinitely, so continuing to run it is a growing security liability, not just an inconvenience.

title: Given a scenario, perform OS installations and upgrades in a diverse environment
tip: GPT vs. MBR and the boot-method list are the two things this objective loves to test as PBQs. Know that GPT is required for drives over 2TB and supports UEFI boot; MBR is legacy/BIOS.
checklist: Boot methods: USB, network, solid-state/flash, internet-based, external/hot-swappable, internal HDD partition, multiboot
Clean install vs. upgrade vs. image deployment vs. remote network install vs. zero-touch deployment
Upgrade considerations: backup files/preferences, app & driver backward compatibility, hardware compatibility
Feature updates and product life cycle

recall.q: A technician is imaging 40 new lab workstations at once with zero manual input at each machine. Which deployment method fits?
Why does a drive larger than 2TB require GPT instead of MBR?
recall.a: MBR's partition table can only address up to 2TB and supports a maximum of 4 primary partitions; GPT removes that size ceiling and supports far more partitions, which is why it's required for large modern drives and UEFI boot.

recall.q: Before upgrading a user's OS in place, what three compatibility checks should you run first?
recall.a: Application/driver backward compatibility, hardware compatibility (CPU/RAM/TPM requirements), and confirming user files/preferences are backed up in case the upgrade needs to be rolled back.

title: Compare and contrast basic features of Microsoft Windows editions
tip: Home vs. Pro is the highest-yield distinction: Pro adds BitLocker, RDP (as host), gpedit.msc, and domain-join — Home has none of those. N versions just mean Media Player/related tech removed for EU compliance, not a feature tier.
checklist: Windows 10 editions: Home, Pro, Pro for Workstations, Enterprise
N versions (EU media-feature-stripped, not a security tier)

recall.q: A user on Windows 10 Home wants to encrypt their drive with BitLocker and can't find the option. Why?
options: BitLocker is Pro-and-above only; Home doesn't include it

recall.q: Which is required for a device to accept incoming Remote Desktop Protocol connections as a host?
options: Any edition, with a registry edit

recall.q: What actually distinguishes an 'N' version of Windows from the standard version?
recall.a: N versions have Windows Media Player and related media technologies stripped out to comply with EU antitrust requirements — it's a regional compliance variant, not a different feature or security tier.

title: Given a scenario, use Microsoft Windows operating system features and tools
tip: The .msc list is pure memorization and shows up constantly as PBQs — know which snap-in solves which symptom (e.g., a service that won't start → services.msc via Task Manager or Computer Management, not Device Manager).
checklist: Task Manager tabs: Services, Startup, Performance, Processes, Users

recall.q: A technician needs to see which startup programs are slowing boot time on Windows 11. Where do they look first?
Which tool would you use to shrink or extend a partition without reformatting the whole drive?
A user reports repeated application crashes but can't describe what's happening. Which tool gives you a timestamped log of the actual error, and how do you open it?
recall.a: Event Viewer, opened via eventvwr.msc — check the Application log for error-level entries around the time of each crash to find the specific fault module or error code.

title: Given a scenario, use the appropriate Microsoft command-line tools
tip: Group these by function instead of memorizing a flat list: navigation (cd/dir), network (ipconfig/ping/netstat/nslookup/tracert/pathping/net use), disk (chkdsk/format/diskpart), file (md/rmdir/robocopy), informational (hostname/whoami/winver), and OS management (sfc/gpupdate/gpresult). sfc and diskpart are the two most commonly tested for actual repair scenarios.
checklist: Network: ipconfig, ping, netstat, nslookup, net use, tracert, pathping
Informational: hostname, net user, winver, whoami, [command] /?

recall.q: A user's system files appear corrupted after a bad shutdown, and File Explorer errors are inconsistent. Which command scans and repairs protected system files?
Which tool would you use to create, delete, and manage disk partitions from the command line?

A Group Policy change was just pushed from the domain controller, but the user's machine hasn't picked it up. What command forces an immediate refresh, and what command lets you verify which policies actually applied?
recall.a: gpupdate /force pushes an immediate refresh of Group Policy; gpresult (e.g., gpresult /r) shows a summary of which policies actually applied to that user/machine, which is the go-to for confirming the push worked.

title: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows settings
tip: This is a long, flat list of Control Panel/Settings categories rather than a conceptually hard objective — treat it as recognition practice: given a symptom, know which settings panel houses the fix (e.g., file extensions not showing → File Explorer Options > View).
checklist: Internet Options, Devices and Printers, Programs and Features
Network and Sharing Center, System, Windows Defender Firewall
Mail, Sound, Device Manager, Indexing Options, Administrative Tools
File Explorer Options: view hidden files, hide extensions, general/view options
Power Options: hibernate, power plans, sleep/suspend, standby, lid-close behavior, fast startup, USB selective suspend
Ease of Access, Time and Language, Update and Security, Personalization
Apps, Privacy, Devices, Network and Internet, Gaming, Accounts

recall.q: A user wants their laptop to stay awake and keep playing music when they close the lid. Which setting controls this?
options: Choose what closing the lid does

recall.q: A user can't see the .docx extension on any of their files and wants ransomware-disguised .exe files to be easier to spot. Where do you fix this?
recall.a: File Explorer Options > View tab — uncheck 'Hide extensions for known file types' so all extensions display.

title: Given a scenario, configure Microsoft Windows networking features on a client/desktop
tip: Static vs. dynamic IP configuration and domain-vs-workgroup are the practical core here — everything else (VPN, proxy, metered connections) is largely recognition-level.
checklist: Domain joined vs. workgroup: shared resources, printers, file servers, mapped drives
Local OS firewall settings: app restrictions/exceptions, configuration
Client network config: IP addressing scheme, DNS, subnet mask, gateway, static vs. dynamic
Establishing connections: VPN, wireless, wired, WWAN/cellular

recall.q: A user's laptop keeps getting a different IP address every time it reconnects, and it needs to stay fixed for a network printer to always find it. What's the fix, and what four values do you need to set manually?
recall.a: Configure a static IP instead of relying on DHCP — you need the IP address itself, the subnet mask, the default gateway, and the DNS server address.

recall.q: Why does Windows ask whether a new network is 'public' or 'private,' and what does that choice actually change?
recall.a: It changes the local firewall profile and network discovery behavior — 'private' relaxes restrictions for trusted home/office networks (file sharing, discoverability), while 'public' locks the machine down for untrusted networks like coffee-shop Wi-Fi.

title: Explain common features and tools of the macOS/desktop operating system
tip: Students coming from Windows-only backgrounds mix up macOS-specific terminology constantly — Finder isn't File Explorer with a different name conceptually (no drive letters, different permissions model), and Keychain/FileVault map to credential-manager/BitLocker concepts but aren't identical.
checklist: App install/uninstall: .dmg, .pkg, .app file types; App Store; uninstall process
Best practices: backups, antivirus, updates/patches, Rapid Security Response (RSR)
System Settings: Displays, Networks, Printers, Scanners, Privacy, Accessibility, Time Machine
Features: multiple desktops, Mission Control, Keychain, Spotlight, iCloud (iMessage/FaceTime/Drive), Gestures, Finder, Dock, Continuity
Disk Utility, FileVault, Terminal, Force Quit

recall.q: A Mac user wants to encrypt their entire startup disk. Which macOS feature is the equivalent of Windows BitLocker?
Which macOS feature stores and auto-fills saved passwords and Wi-Fi credentials system-wide?
What is Rapid Security Response (RSR) on macOS, and why does it matter separately from a normal OS update?
recall.a: RSR is a lightweight, fast-deploying patch mechanism Apple uses to push urgent security fixes between full OS updates, without requiring a full system update/restart cycle — it matters because it closes critical vulnerabilities faster than waiting for the next major point release.

title: Identify common features and tools of the Linux client/desktop operating system
tip: High-yield and easy to over- or under-study — group commands by task the same way as the Windows CLI objective: file management (ls/pwd/mv/cp/rm/chmod/chown/grep/find), package management (apt/dnf), network (ip/ping/curl/dig/traceroute), and know /etc/passwd vs /etc/shadow cold, since that pairing is a favorite exam trap.
checklist: File management: ls, pwd, mv, cp, rm, chmod, chown, grep, find
Network: ip, ping, curl, dig, traceroute
Informational: man, cat, top, ps, du, df

recall.q: Which Linux file stores actual hashed user passwords, as opposed to just usernames and account metadata?
A technician needs to change file permissions on a script so the owner can execute it. Which command does that?
What's the practical difference between su and sudo, and why is sudo generally the safer choice for day-to-day admin tasks?
recall.a: su switches you to another user account entirely (typically root) for the whole session, while sudo runs a single command with elevated privileges and then returns to your normal account — sudo limits the blast radius of a mistake and creates a clearer audit trail of exactly which commands were run as root.

title: Given a scenario, install applications according to requirements
tip: This is a requirements-gathering objective, not a deep technical one — the exam wants you to recognize which system spec (RAM, CPU, VRAM, storage, 32 vs 64-bit) would block an install, and which distribution method (physical media, ISO, downloadable package, image deployment) fits a given scenario.
checklist: System requirements: 32 vs 64-bit, dedicated vs. integrated graphics, VRAM, RAM, CPU, external hardware tokens, storage, app-to-OS compatibility
Distribution methods: physical media/mountable ISO, downloadable package, image deployment
Impact considerations for new apps: device, network, operation, business

recall.q: A user tries to install a 64-bit-only application on an older machine and it fails immediately. What should you check first?
recall.a: Whether the installed OS itself is 32-bit or 64-bit — a 64-bit application cannot run on a 32-bit OS regardless of the CPU's actual capability, so confirm the OS architecture before troubleshooting anything else.

recall.q: Before rolling out a new line-of-business application across 200 workstations, what four categories of impact should be considered beyond 'does it install'?
recall.a: Device impact (resource load on each machine), network impact (bandwidth/licensing calls), operational impact (workflow disruption during rollout), and business impact (cost, downtime, compliance).

title: Given a scenario, install and configure cloud-based productivity tools
tip: Straightforward recall of SaaS productivity categories — email, storage/sync, collaboration tools (spreadsheets, videoconferencing, presentations, word processing, IM), identity sync, and licensing assignment. Low depth, quick review.
checklist: Collaboration tools: spreadsheets, videoconferencing, presentation, word processing, instant messaging

recall.q: A company wants new employees to automatically get the correct Microsoft 365 apps the moment their account is created, without an admin manually assigning each one. What handles this?
recall.a: Licensing assignment tied to identity — typically through group-based licensing where the user's account is added to a group and the license (and associated app access) is applied automatically.

title: Summarize various security measures and their purposes
tip: This objective packs physical security, logical security, and authentication concepts into one list — the biggest trap is MFA factor types (email, hardware token, authenticator app, SMS, voice call, TOTP, OTP) getting confused with each other. Know that TOTP is time-based and app-generated; OTP/passcode is broader and can be delivered any way.
checklist: Physical security: bollards, access control vestibule, badge reader, video surveillance, alarm systems, motion sensors, door locks, equipment locks, guards, fences
Physical access: key fobs, smart cards, mobile digital key, biometrics (retina/fingerprint/palm/facial/voice), lighting, magnetometers
Logical security: least privilege, Zero Trust, ACLs, MFA (email/hardware token/authenticator app/SMS/voice/TOTP/OTP), SAML, SSO

recall.q: Which MFA method generates a new code every 30-60 seconds directly on the user's device without needing cell signal?
A security policy grants a contractor access to a sensitive system only for the two hours they need it, then automatically revokes it. What model does this describe?
What's the core principle behind Zero Trust, and how does it differ from a traditional perimeter-based security model?
recall.a: Zero Trust assumes no user or device is inherently trustworthy, even inside the network perimeter, so every access request is verified regardless of origin — traditional models trust anything already inside the firewall by default, which Zero Trust treats as a flawed assumption.

title: Given a scenario, configure and apply basic Microsoft Windows OS security settings
tip: NTFS vs. share permissions is the single most commonly confused pairing in this objective — share permissions apply only over the network, NTFS permissions apply locally AND over the network, and when both exist together, the MORE restrictive one wins.
checklist: Firewall: activate/deactivate, port security, application security
User/groups: local vs. Microsoft account, standard, administrator, guest, power user
Log-in options: password, PIN, fingerprint, facial recognition, SSO, Windows Hello
NTFS vs. share permissions: file/folder attributes, inheritance
Run as administrator vs. standard user; UAC
Active Directory: joining domain, log-in scripts, moving OUs, home folders, Group Policy, security groups, folder redirection

recall.q: A file has NTFS permissions set to 'Full Control' for a user, but the share permission on the folder it lives in is set to 'Read Only.' What access does the user actually get when connecting over the network?
recall.a: Read Only — when NTFS and share permissions conflict, the more restrictive of the two always wins for network access. Locally (not over the network), only NTFS permissions apply.

recall.q: Which built-in Windows account should always be disabled or renamed as a hardening step?
What does UAC actually protect against, and why does it prompt even for an administrator account?
recall.a: UAC prevents software (including malware) from silently making system-level changes without explicit user consent — it prompts even administrators because admin accounts run with standard-user privileges by default until elevation is explicitly approved, limiting the damage a compromised session or malicious process can do.

title: Compare and contrast wireless security protocols and authentication methods
tip: WPA3 > WPA2 > TKIP is the encryption progression to know cold — TKIP is deprecated/weak and shouldn't appear in any modern recommendation. RADIUS vs. TACACS+ is the other common mix-up: RADIUS encrypts only the password in transit, TACACS+ encrypts the entire packet.

recall.q: Which wireless security protocol should never be recommended for a modern deployment due to known cryptographic weaknesses?
What's the practical difference between RADIUS and TACACS+ that would make an admin choose one over the other for network device authentication?
recall.a: RADIUS encrypts only the password portion of the authentication packet and combines authentication/authorization into one step, while TACACS+ encrypts the entire packet and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting — TACACS+ is generally preferred for administrative access to network devices because of that fuller encryption and granularity.

title: Summarize types of malware and tools/methods for detection, removal, and prevention
tip: Rootkit vs. Trojan vs. fileless malware is the classic confusion trio: a Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software, a rootkit hides at a privileged system level to conceal other malware, and fileless malware lives in memory/scripts without ever writing a file to disk — which is exactly why traditional signature-based antivirus struggles with it.
checklist: Malware types: Trojan, rootkit, virus, spyware, ransomware, keylogger, boot sector virus, cryptominer, stalkerware, fileless
Tools/methods: Recovery Console/environment, EDR, MDR, XDR, antivirus, anti-malware, email security gateway, software firewalls, user education/antiphishing training, OS reinstallation

recall.q: Malware that hides deep in the OS to conceal the presence of other malicious processes, often surviving even a reinstall attempt if not fully removed, is called a:
Which type of malware operates entirely in memory using legitimate system tools/scripts, leaving no file for traditional antivirus to scan?
What's the functional difference between EDR and XDR that a technician should know when recommending a detection solution?
recall.a: EDR (endpoint detection and response) focuses detection and response on individual endpoints/devices, while XDR (extended detection and response) correlates data across endpoints, network, email, and cloud sources into one unified view — XDR gives broader visibility across the whole environment, not just a single device.

title: Compare and contrast common social engineering attacks, threats, and vulnerabilities
tip: The phishing sub-types (vishing, smishing, QR code phishing, spear phishing, whaling) are almost always tested by delivery channel or target, not by name recognition — voice=vishing, SMS=smishing, QR=QR code phishing, targeted individual=spear phishing, targeted executive=whaling.
checklist: Social engineering: phishing (vishing, smishing, QR code phishing, spear phishing, whaling), shoulder surfing, tailgating, impersonation, dumpster diving
Threats: DoS, DDoS, evil twin, zero-day, spoofing, on-path attack, brute-force, dictionary attack, insider threat, SQL injection, XSS, BEC, supply chain/pipeline attack
Vulnerabilities: non-compliant systems, unpatched systems, unprotected systems, EOL, BYOD

recall.q: An attacker sends a phishing email specifically crafted to target a company's CFO, referencing real internal project names to seem legitimate. This is:
A rogue Wi-Fi access point is set up with the same SSID as a coffee shop's legitimate network to intercept traffic. This is an example of a(n):

An employee receives an invoice-payment email that appears to come from their own CEO's real email address, urgently requesting a wire transfer. What's this attack called, and what makes it different from generic phishing?
recall.a: Business email compromise (BEC) — it's different because it typically involves a compromised or convincingly spoofed executive account and targets a specific financial process, relying on authority and urgency rather than a generic mass-phishing lure.

title: Given a scenario, implement procedures for basic SOHO malware removal
tip: This is a strict 10-step ordered process and shows up as a drag-and-drop/ordering PBQ almost every time. Memorize the sequence, not just the steps — quarantine comes before remediation, and re-enabling System Restore is the second-to-last step, not the first.
checklist: 6. Scan and removal techniques (safe mode, preinstallation environment)
9. Enable System Restore and create a restore point

recall.q: Why must System Restore be disabled early in the malware removal process, before scanning and remediation?
recall.a: If System Restore stays active, restore points created while the system was already infected can preserve or reintroduce the malware — disabling it prevents the infection from surviving cleanup via a restore point rollback.

recall.q: Put these three steps in the correct order: (a) reimage/reinstall, (b) update anti-malware software, (c) quarantine the infected system.
recall.a: Quarantine the infected system first (isolate it from the network to stop spread), then update anti-malware software (so scans use current definitions), then reimage/reinstall if remediation and scanning don't fully resolve it.

title: Given a scenario, apply workstation security options and hardening techniques
tip: Treat this as a hardening checklist rather than isolated facts — for any workstation hardening scenario, run through: encryption, passwords, BIOS/UEFI password, account lockout policy, and disabling what's unused (AutoRun, guest account, unused services).
checklist: Password considerations: length, character types, uniqueness, complexity, expiration
End-user best practices: screensaver locks, log off when not in use, secure hardware/PII/passwords, password managers
Account management: restrict permissions, restrict log-in times, disable guest account, failed-attempts lockout, timeout/screen lock, account expiration
Change default admin credentials; disable AutoRun; disable unused services

recall.q: A workstation in a shared lab keeps getting infected via auto-launching USB drives. What single setting change addresses this directly?
recall.a: Disable AutoRun — this stops removable media from automatically executing programs the moment it's inserted, which is a common malware vector in shared/public machines.

recall.q: Why is a BIOS/UEFI password considered a separate hardening layer from the Windows login password?
recall.a: A BIOS/UEFI password protects the firmware level itself — it prevents someone from booting to alternate media, changing boot order, or accessing firmware settings to bypass the OS login entirely, which a Windows password alone can't stop.

title: Given a scenario, apply common methods for securing mobile devices
tip: MDM policy scenarios (BYOD vs. corporate-owned) are the highest-yield part — know that MDM can fully wipe a corporate device but typically only wipes the work container/profile on a BYOD device, same distinction as Core 1's mobile device objective but from the security-hardening angle instead.
checklist: Hardening: device encryption, screen locks (facial, PIN, fingerprint, pattern, swipe), configuration profiles
Patch management: OS updates, app updates
Endpoint security software: antivirus, anti-malware, content filtering
Locator apps, remote wipes, remote backup apps, failed log-in restrictions
Policies: MDM, BYOD vs. corporate-owned, profile security requirements

recall.q: An employee's corporate-owned phone is lost. IT wants to remotely erase everything on it immediately. Is this possible, and what tool enables it?
recall.a: Yes — MDM (mobile device management) on a corporate-owned device typically allows a full remote wipe of the entire device, since the organization owns and fully manages it (unlike BYOD, where wipe is usually limited to the managed work container).

recall.q: Which mobile hardening feature is specifically designed to locate a lost or stolen device on a map?

title: Compare and contrast common data destruction and disposal methods
tip: Know which methods are truly irreversible (physical destruction) vs. reversible with the right tools (standard formatting doesn't actually erase data, it just marks it as available). Degaussing only works on magnetic media (HDDs), not SSDs.
checklist: Physical destruction: drilling, shredding, degaussing, incineration
Recycling/repurposing best practices: erasing/wiping, low-level formatting, standard formatting
Outsourcing: third-party vendor, certification of destruction/recycling

recall.q: Why is degaussing NOT an effective method for destroying data on an SSD?
options: SSDs are too small to degauss
SSDs don't store data magnetically like HDDs do, so degaussing has no effect
Degaussing only works on optical media
SSDs are immune to all forms of data destruction

recall.q: A user thinks a 'standard format' of their old hard drive is enough to make the data unrecoverable before donating the PC. Are they right?
recall.a: No — a standard format just marks the space as available and rebuilds the file system table without actually erasing the underlying data, so recovery tools can often still retrieve it. For real irreversible removal, they'd need secure wiping (multiple-pass overwrite), a low-level format, or physical destruction.

title: Given a scenario, apply security settings on SOHO wireless and wired networks
tip: This overlaps heavily with general router hardening from Core 1's networking domain but from a pure security lens — changing default passwords and disabling UPnP/unused ports are the two most commonly tested 'first steps' in a SOHO hardening scenario.
checklist: Router settings: change default passwords, IP filtering, firmware updates, content filtering, physical placement/secure locations, UPnP, screened subnet, secure management access
Wireless specific: change SSID, disable SSID broadcast, encryption settings, guest access
Firewall settings: disable unused ports, port forwarding/mapping

recall.q: A new SOHO router is being deployed. What are the first two settings a technician should change before anything else, and why?
recall.a: Change the default administrator password (default credentials are publicly known and the single most common attack vector on consumer routers) and disable UPnP (it can let devices/malware open ports automatically without admin awareness) — both close obvious, well-known attack surfaces before any other configuration happens.

recall.q: Why might a technician disable SSID broadcast on a SOHO network?
options: It hides the network name from casual discovery, though it's not a strong security control on its own

title: Given a scenario, configure relevant security settings in a browser
tip: Mostly recognition-level — know that a valid certificate (HTTPS padlock) confirms encrypted transport and identity verification of the site, not that the site's content is safe or trustworthy, and know where each browser setting (pop-up blocker, clearing cache, private browsing, secure DNS) actually lives.
checklist: Browser download/install: trusted vs. untrusted sources, hashing
Settings: pop-up blocker, clearing browsing data/cache, private-browsing mode, sign-in/data sync, ad blockers, proxy, secure DNS
Browser feature management: enable/disable plug-ins, extensions, features

recall.q: A user sees a certificate warning when visiting a familiar banking site and asks if it's safe to click through. What should you tell them, and why?
recall.a: Don't click through — a certificate warning means the browser can't verify the site's identity or that the connection is properly encrypted, which could mean an expired cert, a misconfigured server, or an active on-path/spoofing attack. It's safer to close the tab and navigate to the site independently to confirm.

recall.q: What does a valid HTTPS certificate actually guarantee, and what does it NOT guarantee?
recall.a: It guarantees the connection is encrypted in transit and that the site's identity has been verified by a certificate authority — it does NOT guarantee the site's content is trustworthy, safe, or free of malicious material; plenty of phishing sites use valid HTTPS certificates too.

title: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common Windows OS issues
tip: This is symptom-to-cause matching, the same pattern Core 1's hardware troubleshooting domain used — don't memorize the list as isolated terms, practice mapping each symptom to its most likely first diagnostic step (e.g., BSOD → check Event Viewer/minidump before assuming hardware failure).

recall.q: A user's PC gives a BSOD once or twice a week with no obvious pattern. What's the first thing to check, and why start there instead of reinstalling Windows?
recall.a: Check Event Viewer for the minidump/stop code details around the crash time — the stop code usually points to a specific driver or hardware subsystem (RAM, disk, GPU driver), and reinstalling Windows blindly wastes time if the root cause is a failing driver or bad RAM that will just corrupt the new install too.

recall.q: A desktop reports 'No OS found' on boot after a power outage. What's the most likely first thing to check?
A user's clock keeps drifting and losing several minutes a day, causing certificate and login errors. What's the likely cause and fix?
recall.a: A failing CMOS battery or a misconfigured/blocked NTP time sync — replace the CMOS battery if it's hardware-related, or verify the system's time sync settings/NTP server access if it's software-related; either way, time drift like this commonly breaks certificate validation and domain authentication, which explains the downstream errors.

title: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common mobile OS and application issues
tip: Mostly overlaps conceptually with Core 1's mobile device troubleshooting but focused purely on OS/app-level symptoms rather than hardware — battery life and connectivity issues (Bluetooth/Wi-Fi/NFC) are the highest-yield scenario types.
checklist: Application fails to launch / close / update / install

recall.q: A user's phone battery drains far faster than normal starting right after installing a new app. What's the most likely cause and first troubleshooting step?
recall.a: The new app is likely running excessive background processes or has a location/network permission it's abusing — check battery usage stats per app first to confirm the culprit, then review or revoke that app's background/location permissions rather than assuming a hardware battery failure.

recall.q: A phone's screen won't rotate even though auto-rotate is confirmed enabled in settings. What's a likely non-software cause to also check?

title: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common mobile OS and application security issues
tip: The confusion trap here is distinguishing legitimate performance symptoms (3.2) from security-caused symptoms that look similar — high network traffic, degraded response time, and unexpected battery drain can indicate malware/spyware, not just a buggy app, especially paired with unofficial app store installs or root/jailbreak.
checklist: Security concerns: unofficial app stores, developer mode, root access/jailbreak, unauthorized/malicious apps, application spoofing

Common symptoms: high network traffic, degraded response time, data-usage limit notification, limited/no internet connectivity, high number of ads, fake security warnings, unexpected app behavior, leaked personal files/data

recall.q: A user's phone shows unusually high data usage and unexpected pop-up 'security warnings' urging them to call a number. What's actually happening, and what should the user NOT do?
recall.a: This is almost certainly a scareware/fake-antivirus scam, often delivered through a malicious or spoofed app — the user should not call the number or click the warning, since it's designed to trick them into installing more malware or giving up payment/personal info. The high data usage points to something already running in the background exfiltrating data or downloading more payloads.

recall.q: A user jailbroke/rooted their phone to install apps outside the official store. What security risk does this primarily introduce?
options: Bypassing the OS's built-in app sandboxing and security restrictions, increasing exposure to malicious apps
No real risk if the apps are free
Voids the warranty but is otherwise safe

title: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common personal computer (PC) security issues
tip: Browser-related symptoms (random pop-ups, certificate warnings, redirection, degraded browser performance) get confused with general system infection symptoms — know that browser-specific symptoms often point to a malicious extension or browser hijacker rather than a full system-level infection, which changes the remediation approach.
checklist: Common symptoms: unable to access network, desktop alerts, false AV alerts, altered/missing/renamed system files, inability to access files, unwanted OS notifications, OS update failures
Browser-related symptoms: random/frequent pop-ups, certificate warnings, redirection, degraded browser performance

recall.q: A user reports their browser keeps redirecting Google searches to unfamiliar sites, but the rest of the system seems to run fine. Where should you look first, and why not jump straight to a full malware scan?
recall.a: Check the browser's installed extensions/add-ons first — search redirection is a classic symptom of a malicious or hijacked browser extension, which is often faster and more targeted to remove than running a full system-wide malware scan, though a scan is still worth doing afterward to rule out anything deeper.

recall.q: A user gets a legitimate-looking pop-up claiming their antivirus is out of date and urging an immediate 'update' download. This is most likely:
options: A false/scareware alert designed to trick the user into installing malware

recall.q: Several personal files on a user's PC have suddenly gone missing or been renamed with strange extensions. What should you suspect, and what's the priority action?
recall.a: Suspect ransomware — the priority is to immediately isolate the machine from the network (disconnect Wi-Fi/Ethernet) to stop it from encrypting shared drives or spreading further, before attempting any remediation or restore.

title: Given a scenario, implement best practices associated with documentation and support systems information management
tip: Ticketing-system fields and document-type recognition are both straightforward recall — the exam usually gives you a scenario and asks which document type or ticket field applies, not abstract definitions.
checklist: Ticketing systems: user info, device info, description of issues, categories, severity, escalation levels, clear/concise communication (issue description, progress notes, issue resolution)
Asset management: inventory lists, CMDB, asset tags/IDs, procurement life cycle, warranty/licensing, assigned users
Document types: incident reports, SOPs (incl. software package custom install procedure), new user/onboarding checklist, user off-boarding checklist, SLAs (internal/external), knowledge base/articles

recall.q: A recurring issue keeps getting escalated to Tier 2 with no clear notes on what Tier 1 already tried. What ticketing field/practice is being neglected, and why does it matter?
recall.a: Progress notes / clear written communication on the ticket — without documenting what's already been tried, each escalation forces the next technician to start from scratch, wasting time and risking repeated failed attempts.

recall.q: A document listing every laptop's asset tag, assigned user, warranty expiration, and purchase date is an example of:

title: Given a scenario, apply change management procedures
tip: Standard vs. normal vs. emergency change type is the classic confusion point: standard changes are pre-approved/low-risk and routine, normal changes go through the full change board review, and emergency changes bypass normal approval because of urgent risk — but still require documentation and after-the-fact review.
checklist: Documented business processes: rollback plan, backup plan, sandbox testing, responsible staff members
Change management: request forms, purpose/scope of change
Date/time of change: change freeze, maintenance windows
Change board approvals, implementation, peer review, end-user acceptance

recall.q: A critical zero-day patch needs to be deployed tonight without waiting for the next change board meeting. This is a:
Why does every proposed change need a documented rollback plan before implementation, even for a change the team is confident about?
recall.a: Because if the change causes unexpected issues in production, a rollback plan lets the team quickly restore the previous known-good state rather than troubleshooting live under pressure — 'confident' changes still fail sometimes, and having no rollback plan turns a recoverable mistake into extended downtime.

title: Given a scenario, implement workstation backup and recovery methods
tip: Full vs. incremental vs. differential is the single highest-yield confusion point in this objective: incremental backs up only what changed since the LAST backup (any type) and is fastest to create but slowest to restore; differential backs up everything changed since the LAST FULL backup, so it's a middle ground on both speed and restore time.
checklist: Backup types: full, incremental, differential, synthetic full
Backup rotation: onsite vs. offsite, Grandfather-Father-Son (GFS), 3-2-1 rule

recall.q: Which backup type only captures changes made since the most recent backup of any kind (full or incremental)?
Explain the 3-2-1 backup rule in your own words.
recall.a: Keep at least 3 total copies of your data, stored on 2 different types of media, with at least 1 copy stored offsite — this protects against media failure, local disasters, and site-wide incidents all at once, rather than relying on a single point of failure.

recall.q: A company restores from an incremental backup chain after a server failure. Why does the restore take longer than restoring from a full backup taken the same day would?
recall.a: Because an incremental restore has to reassemble the last full backup PLUS every incremental backup taken since, applying them in sequence — the more incrementals in the chain, the longer and more failure-prone the restore process becomes, compared to a differential or a same-day full backup.

title: Given a scenario, use common safety procedures
tip: Low-conceptual-difficulty, high-recognition objective — the exam mostly wants you to match a safety hazard scenario to the correct control (e.g., static risk → ESD strap/mat, not safety goggles).
checklist: Component handling/storage, cable management, antistatic bags
Personal safety: disconnect power before repair, lifting technique, fire safety, safety goggles, air filter mask

recall.q: A technician is about to install RAM into a desktop. What two ESD precautions should they take before touching the component?
recall.a: Wear an ESD strap connected to a grounded point (or work on an ESD mat), and touch a grounded metal surface (like the case chassis) before handling the RAM — this discharges static buildup that could otherwise silently damage sensitive components.

title: Summarize environmental impacts and local environment controls
tip: MSDS disposal rules (batteries, toner) and power protection devices (UPS vs. surge suppressor) are the two testable clusters — know that a UPS provides battery backup during an outage, while a surge suppressor only protects against voltage spikes and provides no backup power.
checklist: MSDS documentation: proper disposal of batteries, toner, other devices/assets
Temperature/humidity awareness, ventilation, location/equipment placement, dust cleanup, compressed air/vacuums

recall.q: During a power outage, which device keeps a server running for a short period so it can shut down gracefully?
Why can't used toner cartridges just be thrown in regular trash?
recall.a: Toner contains fine particulate and chemical residues that are considered hazardous or regulated waste in many jurisdictions — MSDS guidance requires proper recycling or disposal through certified channels rather than standard trash, both for environmental compliance and safety.

title: Explain the importance of prohibited content/activity and privacy, licensing, and policy concepts
tip: Chain of custody and order of volatility are the highest-yield items here, carried over conceptually from CySA+ but tested at a lighter, more procedural level — know that order of volatility means collecting the MOST volatile evidence first (RAM before disk, disk before backups) since it disappears fastest.
checklist: Incident response: chain of custody, informing management/law enforcement, copy of drive (integrity/preservation), incident documentation, order of volatility
Licensing/DRM/EULA: valid licenses, perpetual license, personal vs. corporate use, open-source license
Regulated data: credit card info, gov-issued ID, PII, healthcare data, data retention requirements

recall.q: A technician investigating a policy violation seizes a workstation. What's the purpose of maintaining chain of custody documentation for that machine going forward?
recall.a: Chain of custody creates a documented, unbroken record of who had possession of the evidence and when, which is essential if the case leads to legal or disciplinary action — without it, the integrity of the evidence can be challenged and potentially thrown out.

recall.q: When collecting digital evidence, which should be captured FIRST, according to order of volatility?

title: Given a scenario, use proper communication techniques and professionalism
tip: This is soft-skills scenario recognition, same style as Core 1's customer-service-adjacent content — the exam gives a difficult-customer scenario and asks what NOT to do (argue, dismiss, be judgmental) as often as what to do.
checklist: Avoid jargon/acronyms/slang; positive attitude; active listening; cultural sensitivity; professional titles
Punctuality; avoid distractions (personal calls, texting, interruptions)
Handling difficult customers: don't argue/be defensive, don't dismiss issues, don't be judgmental, clarify with open-ended questions
Set/meet expectations, offer repair/replacement options, provide documentation, follow up

recall.q: A frustrated customer interrupts you repeatedly and raises their voice about a recurring issue. What's the correct professional response, and what should you avoid doing?
recall.a: Stay calm, actively listen without interrupting back, and use open-ended questions to clarify and restate the issue to show you understand it — avoid arguing, getting defensive, or dismissing their frustration, since escalating back only makes the interaction worse and reflects poorly regardless of who's 'right.'

title: Explain the basics of scripting
tip: Match file extension to language/platform, and don't skip the 'other considerations' section — it's tested as often as the extensions themselves. A script that looks correct can still unintentionally introduce malware, change system settings, or crash a system through resource mishandling.
checklist: Use cases: basic automation, restarting machines, remapping network drives, app installation, automated backups, gathering info/data, initiating updates
Risks: unintentionally introducing malware, inadvertently changing system settings, browser/system crashes from resource mishandling

recall.q: Which script file extension is native to Windows PowerShell?
Which script file extension would you expect to run natively in a Linux/bash environment?
A technician downloads and runs an unfamiliar .bat script from a forum to 'fix' a slow PC, without reading it first. What's the risk, beyond it simply not working?
recall.a: Running an unreviewed script gives it the same permissions the technician has — it could unintentionally (or maliciously) change system settings, delete files, or introduce malware, since batch scripts can execute arbitrary system commands with no built-in safety checks.

title: Given a scenario, use remote access technologies
tip: RDP vs. VNC vs. SSH is the core distinction: RDP is Windows-native full remote desktop, VNC is cross-platform remote desktop (generally less secure by default), and SSH is command-line-only, not a GUI remote desktop protocol at all — a common exam trap is treating SSH as if it gives graphical access.
checklist: Methods/tools: RDP, VPN, VNC, SSH, RMM, SPICE, WinRM
Third-party tools: screen-sharing, videoconferencing, file transfer, desktop management software
Security considerations of each access method

recall.q: Which remote access protocol provides command-line-only access and does NOT provide a graphical desktop by itself?

An IT team manages hundreds of endpoints remotely for patching, monitoring, and scripted maintenance — not just one-off support sessions. Which category of tool fits this best, and how is it different from a basic RDP session?
recall.a: RMM (remote monitoring and management) — unlike a one-to-one RDP session for interactive support, RMM tools are built for managing many endpoints at scale, running scheduled scripts, monitoring health, and pushing patches without needing an interactive session on each machine.

title: Explain basic concepts related to artificial intelligence (AI)
tip: New objective for this exam version — expect it to be tested lightly but directly. Know the core limitations (bias, hallucinations, accuracy) and the private-vs-public data distinction, since that's the practical IT-support angle: what happens to company data when an employee pastes it into a public AI tool.
checklist: Private vs. public: data security, data source, data privacy

recall.q: An employee pastes a customer's PII into a free public AI chatbot to help draft a response. What's the practical data risk here, from an IT support standpoint?
recall.a: Data entered into a public AI tool may be stored, logged, or used to train the model outside the company's control, which can violate data privacy policy and regulatory requirements around PII — this is exactly why organizations often require using only approved, private/enterprise AI tools where data handling is contractually controlled.
